title: Promotion of electrochemical CO2 reduction to ethylene on phosphorus-doped copper nanocrystals with stable Cuδ+ sites
abstract: Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to C2+ products is a sustainable energy-driven pursuit for high added-value hydrocarbons. Tremendous efforts have been made to copper based electrocatalysts, which are well-known for producing C2+ products. However, being short of well-defined catalysts with stable Cuδ+ electronic structure hinders its practical application and in-depth understanding. Herein, we developed a facile one-pot approach to prepare Cuδ+-rich catalyst by doping phosphorus. Enhanced performance and tunable product selectivities are achieved due to the electron donor–acceptor interaction based on phosphorus content in series. C2 hydrocarbons and alcohols are produced with high (~44.9%) selectivity, in which C2H4 (30.7 ± 0.9%) is dominant at − 1.6 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). This P-Cu catalyst shows a significantly higher current density (57.2 mA cm 2) compared to pristine Cu. In addition, the favorable Cuδ+ is reserved during CO2RR contributing to a longterm stability. Experimental results and DFT calculations demonstrate that the Cuδ+ moiety facilitates the adsorption of carbon intermediates, C-C coupling and hence promotes the generation of C2H4 energetically. The well-designed catalyst indicates the profit of electronic structure engineering in designing catalysts for multiplestep chemical conversions.

A B S T R A C T
Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to C2+ products is a sustainable energy-driven pursuit for high added-value hydrocarbons. Tremendous efforts have been made to copper based electrocatalysts, which are well-known for producing C2+ products. However, being short of well-defined catalysts with stable Cuδ+ electronic structure hinders its practical application and in-depth understanding. Herein, we developed a facile one-pot approach to prepare Cuδ+-rich catalyst by doping phosphorus. Enhanced performance and tunable product selectivities are achieved due to the electron donor–acceptor interaction based on phosphorus content in series. C2 hydrocarbons and alcohols are produced with high (~44.9%) selectivity, in which C2H4 (30.7 ± 0.9%) is dominant at − 1.6 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The continuous emission of anthropogenic CO2 has led to the vital concern of CO2 utilization, which produces value-added chemical feedstocks and mitigates the environment problems [1]. The electrochemical CO2RR is an emerging route with great interests for the process can be driven by off-peak electricity or intermittent renewable energy sources [2]. However, because of the high stability of CO2 and sluggish multi-electron transfer kinetics, CO2RR requires large overpotential and will produce multiple products such as ethylene, ethanol and other C2+ products [3]. To increase the selectivity and realize the practicality, unique electrocatalysts with high hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) overpotentials have been developed. Cu is proven to be the mostly used heterogeneous catalyst that tends to produce high value and energydense hydrocarbons and alcohols but with low yield and selectivity [4].
Studies with Cu-electrodes have demonstrated the different reactivity and selectivity by controlling the morphology, particle size,
surface structure, and high-local pH of the electrode [5]. For example, it has been reported that branched copper oxide nanoparticles promoted high selectivity of ethylene compared with pristine Cu [6]. On Cu (100) base plane, the formation of ethylene is predominant while CH4 on Cu (111). Gattrell et al. found that the step atom present on Cu (100) could favor C-C bond coupling [7]. The introduction of nitride into Cu with perovskite structure (Cu3N) can stabilize the Cu(I) active site on the (100) plane and further enhance the selectivity to ethylene [8]. To increase the pH near Cu electrodes can accelerate the reduction of the intermediate CO to C2 products [9]. Nevertheless, the overall selectivity and current density towards multi-carbon products in addition to the mechanistic understanding are still limited.
Notably, the electronic structure tuned by the composition in copperbased compound also provides positive complexity to the CO2RR system [5]. As previously reported, high Faradaic efficiencies for C2 products have been achieved by introducing Cuδ+ into copper catalysts. The favored Cuδ+ can be produced by the oxygen content in copper oxide

In addition, surface modification of Cubased catalysts has been proved to be an effective method for constructing Cuδ+. Zhao et al. demonstrated that the presence of phosphate ligands on Cu surface probably facilitates the formation of Cuδ+-Hδ-
[12]. However, the phosphate ligands are able to improve the proton transport and thus enhace the competive HER simultaneously. Therefore, a major step in forming stable Cuδ+ came with the doping of nonmetallic elements such as boron (B) [13], sulfur (S) [14], and nitrogen (N) [15] due to their rich valence electrons. A common feature has been unveiled that the doping will alter the surface electron distribution due to different electronegativity (B: 2.04, S: 2.58, N: 3.04) compared with copper (Cu: 1.9) [16]. Phosphorus (P: 2.19) has a smaller electronegativity than that of nitrogen and sulfur while a larger atomic radius than nitrogen and boron. Remarkably, its electron withdrawing ability is much higher than boron, making it well worth exploring the unique properties of phosphorus doped catalysts. Theoretical studies have demonstrated that phosphorus doping can improve the electron donor properties of carbon materials, accordingly realize an enhanced catalytic activity, e.g. in ORR [17]. These reports demonstrated metal elements would donate electrons to phosphorus in ORR and phosphorus could induce an electron withdrawing effect from metal atoms for improving the electro-oxidation of ethanol [18,19]. Considering the role of phosphorus in altering electronic state of metal elements in the field of oxygen-reduction and oxidation of methanol, ethanol, formic acid [19-23], phosphorus is expected to generate Cuδ+ for enhancing its selectivity of multi-carbon products.
In this study, Cu nanocatalysts Px-Cu (x is doping molar ratio of P:Cu) with different phosphorus doping concentrations were synthesized by a facile coreduction process. Among them, remarkable C2H4 current density with Faradaic efficiency (FE) up to 30.7 ± 0.9% is achieved by the stable Cuδ+ in P0.075-Cu, and total C2 products are produced with ~44.9% selectivity. Compared with pristine copper, the hydrogen generation in CO2RR of P0.075-Cu catalyst was significantly inhibited. It reveals that Cuδ+ spiece is retained during CO2RR. To get insight into the enhancement of CO2RR catalytic performance, DFT calculations further confirm the contribution of doping P by accepting electrons transferred from Cu and optimizing the adsorption of carbon intermediates for favorable C2-products generation.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Copper chloride (CuCl2, 98%) was purchased from Aladdin. Sodium hypophosphite (NaH2PO2, 99%) was purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. Hydrazine hydrate aqueous solution (N2H4⋅H2O, 85%), potassium hydrogen carbonate (KHCO3), potassium hydroxide (KOH), hydrochloric acid (36–38%), ethanol and acetone were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Nafion N-115 membranes (0.180 mm thick, 0.90 meq/g exchange capacity) and Nafion D-521 dispersion (5% w/w in water and 1-propanol, ≥0.92 meq/ g exchange capacity liquid) were purchased from Alfa Aesar. All chemicals were of analytical grade and not further treated.

sections.heading: 2.2. Catalysts preparation
sections.text:
In a typical synthesis of P0.075-Cu (phosphorus doped copper with a molar ratio of 0.075:1), 10 mmol of CuCl2 powder and 1.67 mL HCl were dissolved in 100 mL deionized water with magnetic stirring before 100 mL of 7.5 mM NaH2PO2 solution was added. The mixed solution was transferred into a 500 mL three-necked flask. It was vigorously stirred at 80℃ to form a homogeneous solution. Subsequently, 3 mL N2H4⋅H2O was injected into the flask and heated for another hour under stirring. Finally, the solid suspension was collected by centrifugation, and
cleaned with deionized water, ethanol and acetone, respectively. Then the brown powder was immediately dried under vacuum at 60℃ for overnight. Different concentrations of NaH2PO2 (namely, 5 mM for P0.05-Cu, 10 mM for P0.10-Cu, and 15 mM for P0.15-Cu) were used. The pristine Cu powder in control group was carried out following a similar procedure without NaH2PO2. The samples were immediately stored in a glove box under the protection of argon after preparation and drying.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterization
sections.text: The crystal structures of the samples were characterized by the Philips X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.15418 nm) at a voltage of 40 kV and a current of 40 mA. The scan step size in our experiment is 0.008 in XRD measurements. The morphology and grain size information of the samples were characterized on the field emmission scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi S-4800, equipped with an energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer) and JEM-2100UHR transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100UHR). The XPS was collected on a X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy spectrometer (XPS, Thermo Fisher K-alpha 250Xi) with Al Kα radiation to analyze the surface elemental composition and states. The peak of C 1 s with the position at 284.6 eV was used as a reference to correct the charging effect.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical CO2RR measurements and products analysis
sections.text:
All the electrochemical measurements were conducted with a threeelectrode configuration on CHI 760E Electrochemical Workstation. The electrochemical CO2RR testing was carried out in a gas-tight H-cell with two compartments separated by a piece of proton exchange membrane (Nafion N-115 membrane). For this system KHCO3 with a constant concentration of 0.1 M was used as electrolyte in each compartment with a volume of 30 mL. It was saturated with CO2 before electrochemical tests and the pH value for the electrolyte was 6.8. A platinum plate and a leak-free saturated Ag/AgCl electrode were employed as counter electrode and reference electrode (Hugo Sachs Elektronik Harvard apparatus GmbH), respectively. The actual potential was converted to the RHE reference potential according to eq 1.
ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.197 + 0.059 × pH (1) To prepared the working electrode, 5 mg of the synthesized sample
powder, 120 μL of Nafion D-521 solution (5 wt%), and 1 mL of ethanol were well mixed and ultrasonic for 20 min until a homogeneous ink was obtained. The ink was then loaded on a carbon paper of 0.5 * 1 cm2 with a catalyst loading of 1 mg cm− 2 before being dried at room temperature. When the Amperometric i-t Curve was used to start the electrochemical reduction of CO2, 0.5 mg of catalyst was loaded onto 0.5 * 1 cm2 of carbon paper as the working electrode and placed in the cathode chamber. Before the electrochemical reaction, the electrolyte was presaturated with high purity CO2 (99.999%) for 1 h to achieve CO2 saturation. The cathode worked at a constant potential for 20 min to completely reduce the possible oxidized species and obtained a stable i-t curve before the test. The gas products from CO2RR were analyzed by a gas circulation system (WH500-USB series) with an automatic sampling loop. In addition, the liquid products in the electrolyte were collected and analyzed by NMR instruents (Bruker AVANCEIII-HD series).

sections.heading: 2.5. Theoretical calculations
sections.text:
The density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed with the VASP Package. The electron–ion interactions were represented by the projector-augmented-wave potentials. The Perdew-BurkeErnzerh of exchange–correlation functional within GGA was used. The free energy changes (ΔG) of each elementary reaction step during CO2RR were calculated using the CHE model. (Calculations details in Supporting Information)

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
The Px-Cu (x = 0.05, 0.075, 0.1 and 0.15) nanocrystals were prepared through a facile one-pot approach of reducing CuCl2 in the presence of NaH2PO2 and N2H4⋅H2O. The as-obtained pristine Cu and P0.075Cu were selected for further structural characterization. The crystal structure of P0.075-Cu and pristine Cu was characterized by XRD. As shown in Fig. 1a, three typical diffraction peaks corresponding to (111), (200) and (220) planes of the face-centered cubic copper (PDF#03065-9026) appear for both pristine Cu and P0.075-Cu. There is no characteristic peak assigned to other impurities such as oxidized or phosphated copper. The diffraction peak of phosphorus element is not detected, suggesting the highly dispersed phosphorus species with small doping amount. However, the tiny difference lies in the positions of the diffraction peaks as listed in Table 1. It’s noted that the diffraction peaks of Cu shift slightly to smaller angles after introducing phosphorus elements, and a shift of the diffraction peak of (200) plane is marked in the illustration of Fig. 1a, indicating the lattice expansion of Cu nanostructure with doping [24,25]. Spacing of crystal surfaces collected from the XRD data further confirmed this phenomenon (Table S1, Supplementary Information). The shift profile of Cu characteristic diffraction peaks was further confirmed by a zoom-in of Cu (111) peaks. As shown in Figure S1a, the peaks slightly shift to smaller 2θ values accompanied with the increase of phosphorus content (Px-Cu, x = 0, 0.05, 0.075, 0.10, 0.15) according to a zoom-in of Cu (111) peak in Figure S1b, which further indicates an enlargement in the Cu-Cu interatomic distance.
The morphological and structural characteristics were further investigated by SEM. As shown in Fig. 1b, P0.075-Cu clearly shows the irregular particle structure with a size of 100–500 nm. And SEM images with the same magnification of pristine Cu and P0.075-Cu in Figure S2 and S3 reveal that both the morphology and particle size are essentially unchanged after doping. The distinct lattice spacing of P0.075-Cu was measured to be 0.208 nm (Fig. 1c) and assigned to (111) plane. Furthermore, the selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern (the
inset in Fig. 1c) confirms its polycrystalline character. Representative EDS mapping of P0.075-Cu in Fig. 1d clearly reveals that both copper and phosphorus elements are uniformly dispersed throughout the nanostructure, revealing that phosphorus is successfully incorporated into copper nanostructure during the synthesis.
XPS was measured to further characterize the elemental composition and surface electronic states of the as-prepared catalysts. Cu 2p spectra of pristine Cu and P0.075-Cu before CO2RR are deconvoluted in Fig. 2a. There is a symmetric peak at 932.2 eV corresponding to Cu0 of Cu 2p3/2 in pristine Cu without phosphorus [26]. However, the peak of Cu 2p3/2 in P0.075-Cu is fitted with two states. Besides the characteristic peak of Cu0 at 932.3 eV, another locates at 933.6 eV, which falls in between Cu0 and Cu2+ (934.6 eV). It indicates that the copper in P0.075-Cu is partly electron-deficient with a valence state between 0 and + 2 [27,28]. The peak of Cu 2p1/2 exhibits similar characteristics to that of Cu 2p3/2. As a consequence, the desirable Cuδ+ is formed by introducing phosphorus as the electron-acceptor into Cu [19]. In addition, the doping of phosphorus leads to a shift in the peak of copper to a higher binding energy, which further confirms the the slightly positive state of copper. The broad peaks between 942.4–947.5 eV and 940–945 eV in pristine Cu and P0.075-Cu correspond to the satellite peaks of Cu2+, respectively [29,30]. Obviously, the broad peak of the latter is much stronger than that of the former. Apart from the surface partial oxidation of copper sample, the powerful peak is primarily due to the generation of Cuδ+ in bulk phase or the presence of more oxygen species (Table S2). To further ascertain the oxidation state of copper in P0.075-Cu, Cu LMM Auger spectra were performed on the samples (Figure S4). For the P0.075-Cu, the Auger
H. Chen et al.
Applied Surface Science 544 (2021) 148965
spectrum exhibits an asymmetric and broad peak fitted with two symmetric peaks. The one at 916.6 eV is lower than Cu0 (918 eV) and Cu2+ (917.8 eV), which can be assigned to Cuδ+ [31-33]. Together with the subsequent shoulder peak at 918 eV corresponding to the metallic Cu as that in pristine Cu [34]. The Cu LMM spectra results provided strong evidence for the presence of Cuδ+ in P0.075-Cu, which is in accordance with the XPS spectra. The successful doping of phosphorus species in P0.075-Cu is verified by P 2p spectra as shown in Fig. 2b. The peaks at 129.9 and 130.2 eV can be assigned to elemental state phosphorus (P0) of P 2p3/2 and P 2p1/2 while the fitted P 2p3/2 and P 2p1/2 peaks at 132.9 and 133.6 eV, respectively, correspond to the P bonded to oxygen atom [35-38]. There is a negative shift of 0.5 eV for the main peak at 129.9 eV compared to that of pristine phosphorus (130.4 eV). It may be attributed to that phosphorus accepts electrons from metals in the Px-Cu as Pd-P (-0.3 eV), Mn-P (-0.8 eV) [39,40]. The presence of oxidized phosphorus may be attributed to the side reaction of sodium hypophosphite
during the fabrication. No copper phosphides are detected, indicating the successful formation phosphorus doped copper structure. Table S2 lists the NaH2PO2/CuCl2 ratio in the preparation and the resultant composition of Px-Cu measured by XPS. The atomic ratios of P/Cu in the products are 0.028, 0.055, 0.079, 0.089 corresponding to P0.05-Cu, P0.075-Cu, P0.10-Cu, P0.15-Cu, respectively. The results indicate that phosphorus content was increased with the dosage of NaH2PO2 increasing.
The CO2RR activity of Px-Cu was investigated in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 in a typical H-type electrochemical cell at room temperature. The controlled potential analysis as a function of catalyst composition was carried out. All the resulting gas products were monitored by a gas chromatograph (GC) connected to the electrolytic cell. The liquid products were characterized by 1H NMR spectroscopy. All the potentials were converted and referred to RHE in this work. Table S3 lists the Faradaic efficiencies of ethylene taken on Px-Cu. A significant enhanced
H. Chen et al.
Applied Surface Science 544 (2021) 148965
activity towards ethylene was achieved on P0.075-Cu with the maximum FE of 30.7 ± 0.9% at − 1.6 V. Linear sweep voltammogram (LSV) curves were also measured at a scan rate of 10 mV s− 1 in Ar-saturated and CO2saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 and shown in Fig. 3a. The increase of current density in the Ar-saturated solution can attributed to HER. Obviously, a higher current density performed in CO2-saturated solution on P0.075-Cu indicates that CO2RR is more favorable with respect to HER. The FE of gas products and partial current densities of ethylene at different applied potentials obtained on P0.075-Cu and pristine Cu were further compared in Fig. 3. There are two distinct distribution trends corresponding to CO and C2H4 on P0.075-Cu (Fig. 3b), respectively. At a low potential of − 0.9 V, CO is the main gas product with the highest FE of 41.3 ± 0.8%. With the negative increase of working potential, the FE of CO decreases gradually, while that of C2H4 increases and reaches the maximum of 30.7 ± 0.9% at − 1.6 V. In addition, the undesirable competitive HER is effectively suppressed on P0.075-Cu and the FE of H2 keeps under 25% in a broad potential window of − 0.9 ~ -1.6 V. The gas product distribution obtained on pristine Cu in Fig. 3c prones to vary similarly as P0.075-Cu. However, the FEs of CO and C2H4 are much lower. For example, the maximum FE for C2H4 of only 17.1 ± 0.7% is obtained at − 1.6 V. In addition, gas products of P0.05-Cu, P0.10-Cu and P0.15-Cu of CO2 reduction were also reflected in Figure S5. Among them, the maximum FE of ethylene in P0.05-Cu, P0.10-Cu and P0.15-Cu is 24.2 ± 0.8%, 24.6 ± 0.4% and 23.1 ± 0.7%, respectively. Obviously, the selectivity of ethylene has been improved significantly after doping compared with that of pristine copper. Moreover, the HER is inhibited as the doping amount is relatively low, but the inhibition is remarkably reduced with too many phosphorus atoms. The lowest HER was found on P0.075-Cu along with the optimal CO2RR performance of P0.075-Cu. The selectivity of ethylene on P0.075-Cu is notably high comparing to previously reported copper catalysts (Fig. 3d).
Moreover, we calculated and compared the partial current densities for C2H4 on P0.075-Cu and pristine Cu as shown in Fig. 3e. It increases sharply from − 1.3 V and achieves a summit of 17.57 mA cm− 2 on P0.075Cu at the optimal operating potential of − 1.6 V, which is almost twice as high as that of pristine Cu. Meanwhile, as shown in Figure S6, the total current density of P0.075-Cu catalyst is remarkably larger than that of pristine Cu catalyst at − 1.6 V. Considering the lower FE of H2 on P0.075Cu, it can be concluded that the CO2RR performance to C2H4 is significantly enhanced by phosphorus doping.
The stability of CO2RR of P0.075-Cu electrocatalyst were measured at a constant potential of − 1.6 V for 9000 s. As shown in Fig. 3f, the catalyst displays highly stable catalytic current over the period examined. Accordingly, FE of C2H4 was maintained around 30%, indicating the outstanding stability of P0.075-Cu catalyst at a high current density.
The liquid products were collected after long-term reduction processes on P0.075-Cu and pristine Cu catalysts and detected by 1H NMR spectroscopy. The FEs of all reduction products at varied potetials are
presented in Figure S7 and Figure S8. Formic acid, acetic acid and ethanol were detected. The total Faradaic efficiencies of P0.075-Cu in Figure S7 at the operating potential of − 0.8 ~ -1.7 V are in the range of 95.4–102.4 ± 2.3% revealing that all the major products have been accounted for. Interestingly, the distibution of C1 products and C2 products tends to be adjustable depending on the operating potential. The FE of C1 products at − 0.9 V exceeds 70% along with less than 10% of C2 prodcts. However, the FE of C2 products increases with the potential shifts negatively and reaches the maximum of ~44.9% at − 1.6 V, which is higher than that of pristine Cu (~26.6%) in Fig. S8.
The improved CO2RR performance of P0.075-Cu is attributed to the introduction of Cuδ+ active sites by phosphorus doping, which may promote the adsorption of CO2 molecules and enhance the C-C coupling reactions [13]. To investigate the stability of the favorable electronic structure, the P0.075-Cu catalyst was collected after the long-term CO2RR at − 1.6 V and characterized by XPS. As shown in Fig. 4a, the characteristic peaks of Cu 2p at 932.2 eV and 934.0 eV corresponding to Cu0 and Cuδ+ can be deconvoluted as well. These peaks show minor shifts compared to those of P0.075-Cu obtained before CO2RR, which demonstrates the well maintained electronic structure involving Cuδ+. Additionally, the satellite peak between 942.0 eV and 944.5 eV is flatter compared with the fresh P0.075-Cu sample in XPS spectra, which evidence the reduction of oxidized copper during CO2RR [44-46]. Notably, the characteristic peaks of P 2p3/2 (129.8 and 133.1 eV) and P 2p1/2 (130.4 and 133.4 eV) in P 2p spectra barely change after CO2RR as shown in Fig. 4b. The resultant stable composition and electronic structure of Cuδ+ and phosphorus further confirm the outstanding stability of Cuδ+ in P0.075-Cu catalyst during CO2RR.
To further understand the origin of higher activity over the Cuδ+
active sites induced by homogeneously doping of phosphorus, DFT calculations were carried out to study the electronic structure and energetics of the key step in CO2RR over characteristic P-Cu configurations. Different doping configurations were constructed and optimized as shown in Figure S9. The stable configurations namely Fcc of P-Cu was used for further analysis due to the superiority of the bader chage transfer compared with Hcp in Table S4. The charge density difference and the bader charge analysis are shown in Fig. 5. The charge accumulation near the doped P and neighboring Cu atoms are shown in Fig. 5a. Compared with the perfect Cu (111), the electrons transfer from Cu to P atoms obviously, indicating a strong interaction. The bader charge of the surface Cu atoms turns to be negative on P-Cu but negligibly positive on Cu in Fig. 5b, further confirming the electron transfer from surrounding Cu atoms to the P atom on P-Cu. The variation of electron density between Cu and P atoms facilitates the formation of Cuδ+.
The adsorption degree of reactants and intermediate on catalyst can well reflect the possibility of catalytic reaction path. Firstly, the energetics of CO2, *CO and *COOH adsorbed on the catalyst surface was
H. Chen et al.
Applied Surface Science 544 (2021) 148965
investigated, and their adsorption energy were compared in Table 2. Compared with the adsorption on pristine Cu (111), the carbon intermediates exhibit more stable adsorption with higher adsorption energy on Fcc configuration. Though the adsorption energy of CO2 on the two substrates is small, the *COOH adsorption energy is obviously increased, which shows that the principle of proton-coupled electron transfer (CO2 + e- + H+ + * → *COOH) is satisfied for copper-based materials [47]. The adsorption energy of *CO on Fcc (− 1.13 eV) is about twice as that on Cu (111) (-0.62 eV). It endows the advanced production of C2+ products rather than CO desorption, which is consistent with the experiment results. In general, the C-C coupling includes three pathways: *CO dimerization, *CO → *COH → *COHCO and *CO → *CHO → *CHOCO on copper surface [48]. As the name implies, the dimerization requires neighboring *CO while the two *CO with the optimal adsorption configuration on P-Cu surface are far from each other (4.086 Å) and difficult to dimerize (Figure S10a). Furthermore, by comparing the ΔG for the coupling steps of *CHO → *CHOCO and *COH → *COHCO, the latter is more achievable in geometry and thermodynamics (Figure S10b). Therefore, the coupling pathway of *COH → *COHCO can be concluded, which was further studied by DFT calculations.
The free energies of CO2 towards *COHCO and CO on Cu (111) and P-Cu at different potential were present in Fig. 6a and 6b, respectively. As is well known, the steps with electron shift can be affected by the operating potential while those non-electron transforming steps cannot.
Initially, the free energy changes along the pathways of CO2 → *COOH → *CO → *COH and CO2 → *COOH → *CO → CO are similar on Cu (111) and P-Cu. However, the critical steps of C-C coupling (non-electron transforming step) are absolutely different. The *COH → *COHCO step with a ΔG of 0.51 eV on Cu (111) is difficult while it is easy on P-Cu (ΔG = − 0.49 eV), indicating that P doped Cu is beneficial to produce C2 products. At a low operating potential, e.g. − 0.8 V, CO production on both Cu (111) and P-Cu is competitive to C2 production due to a lower ΔG of *CO → CO than that of *CO → *COH. As the operating potential increasing, e.g. − 1.4 V, the ΔG of electron transforming steps (CO2 → *COOH and *CO → *COH) decreases dramatically, trending to C2 production. Though they are negative for Cu (111) at − 1.4 V, the CO release step is always competitive to the critical coupling step for C2 production at each potential (Fig. 6a). Interestingly, the ΔG of *CO → *COH at − 1.6 V is only − 0.07 eV for P-Cu, resulting an inverse selectivity of C2 production to CO production as the experiment (Fig. 6b).
To get insight into the enhancement mechanism of doping phosphorus, the electronic structure of the catalysts was analyzed by the density of states (DOS). As is displayed in Figure S11a and S11b, the peak of Cu 3d-orbital near the Fermi level is significantly enhanced after doping phosphorus, which indicates phosphorus atoms can effectively regulate the 3d-orbital of copper near the Fermi level. PDOS of *COHCO intermediate adsorbed on Cu (111) and P-Cu were further compared in Figure S12a, S12b. There is a strong overlap between the Cu 3d-orbital in P-Cu catalyst and the *COHCO intermediate near the Fermi energy level, indicating the hybridization of them. Correspondingly, the antibond orbitals above the Fermi energy level were formed between Cu 3d-orbital in P-Cu and *COHCO, which reveals that the intermediate adsorbed more stably on the surface of P-Cu catalyst. Based on the experimental results, the selectivity of C2 products increased with the introduction of phosphorus, especially for ethylene instead of ethanol. The superiority of ethylene over ethanol was compared in calculation. The pathways of ethylene and ethanol have been mentioned in many
H. Chen et al.
Applied Surface Science 544 (2021) 148965
studies [11,49], we focused on the divergence in the pathways of two products. The pH of electrocatalytic environment in this study was close to neutral. Previous researches have demonstrated that the reaction pathways between ethylene and ethanol are mainly determined by the *CCHOH intermediate (pathways to ethylene: *COHCO → *COHCOH → *CCOH → *CCHOH → *CCH → *CHCH → *CHCH2 → *CH2CH2 → C2H4, pathways to ethanol: *COHCO → *COHCOH → *CCOH → *CCHOH → *CCH2OH → *CHCH2OH → *CH2CH2OH → *CH3CH2OH → C2H5OH). Here two reaction pathways are compared to understand the products selectivity. The optimized geometries are illustrated in Figure S13a. The ΔG of *CCOH→*CCHOH step was calculated as − 0.46 eV (Figure S13b). To drive the next hydrogenation step on carbon of C2H5OH, a ΔG of 0.40 eV is required, which is larger than that to form *CCH (ΔG = -0.47 eV) of C2H4. Therefore, ethylene production pathway is more competitive than that of ethanol during CO2RR. All these calculation results further demonstrate that phosphorus doping could endow Cu with an optimal Cuδ+ electronic structure and surface adsorption feature for CO2RR, facilitate the production of C2H4 in CO2 reduction. Further to get insight into the enhancement, adsorption experiments of P0.075-Cu and pristine Cu in Ar-saturated 1 M KOH solution were supplemented to investigate the different binding affinities to OH–. According to the CV curves in Figure S14, the onset potential and peak potential of OH–
adsorption on P0.075-Cu were both lower than those on pristine Cu. It demonstrates that the stronger adsorption affinity of OH– occurs on P0.075-Cu in accordance with adsorption behavior to CO2RR intermediates [50,51].

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, a simple strategy of doping element phosphorus is propsed for constructing the favorable Cuδ+ sites for electrochemical CO2RR, which aims to synthesize C2 products especially C2H4. The CO2RR highly depends on the content of phsphorous and the operating potential. For example, C1 products with >70% FE can be achieved at a low potential of − 0.9 V while C2 products approaches to ~44.9% at a high potential of − 1.6 V on P0.075-Cu. Due to the stable Cuδ+ sites, a high CO2RR current density (57.2 mA cm− 2) and suppressed HER were achieved to reach a high selectivity of C2H4 (30.7 ± 0.9%) as well. The corresponding DFT calculations demonstrates that the favorable Cuδ+
electronic structure induced by doping phosphorus can effectively improve the adsorption ability of carbon intermediates for C-C coupling. Our findings shed the light on careful design of high activity and selectivity of Cu-based catalysts with favorable Cuδ+, especially toward C2 products from CO2.
